headline: IPO valuation unjustifiable at ~$44 billion AUD given only 46MW running, loss-making, versus Crusoe's $140 billion contracted value at a similar ask
reasoning: Firmus went to market seeking $44 million AUD (approximately $30 billion USD), similar to US peer Crusoe Energy which has over $140 billion of contracted value and multi-billion dollar revenues. By contrast, Firmus has only 46MW of capacity running and is still loss-making, making the comparable valuation implausible. The core issue is a valuation mismatch, not a question about whether AI investment is real or durable.
quote: If we look at firms which went to market asking for $44 million dollars, that's about 30 billion US, which is exactly where a company called Crusoe in the US recently raised capital at. And if we look at Crusoe, they've got more than $140 billion of contracted value and the revenues is reportedly in the multi-billion US dollar range. So you compare that to firmus, which has 46MW running, it's still loss making, and it's still incredibly small relative to a company like Crusoe. Yet the valuation that they were asking was very similar. So to us that didn't make sense.
episode_title: The stock caught in crossfire of the Firmus flop

headline: Trimmed or exited after strong gains as forward returns no longer compelling on valuation; rotating toward application layer
reasoning: ELM's global fund has held Nvidia and other AI hardware names which performed very well over recent years. However, Mirchandani says valuations for some of these positions no longer justify the forward returns, prompting reductions and exits. The firm is rotating toward the application layer — software companies with large distribution and existing client bases that are users of AI — as well as industrial and healthcare companies embedding AI in their operations.
quote: In our global fund we've invested in companies like Nvidia, AMD, Micron, Bloom Energy, ARM as well. And they've all done incredibly well over the last few years. But when we look at the valuation, not for all of them, but certainly for some of those stocks, we've down-waited and exited because if we look at the outlook, compare that with the valuation, we think that the forward returns are not compelling anymore. So we've adjusted our portfolio accordingly.

headline: AI data centre build-out to continue but CapEx growth rate likely to moderate as hyperscalers hit leverage limits; US political overhang adding near-term pressure
reasoning: The sector requires and has attracted enormous capital and is expected to continue investing, but the pace of growth may slow. Mirchandani points to the leverage already taken on by the large hyperscalers as a constraint on further capital deployment. Additionally, the US midterm election environment has made AI data centres politically contentious, creating a further overhang. The view is that AI investment is structurally embedded in products and lifestyles and will persist, but the high-growth phase of CapEx may be peaking.
quote: The sector needs a lot of capital. It's invested already a lot of capital and it's likely to continue in the future. And you overlay what's happening in the US with the midterms coming up and AI data centers being such a political point there. So there's been a lot of pushback over there as well. So that's creating this overhang. But in saying that, our view is that the AI investment is here to continue and it's already embedded in our lifestyles and products. And so the quantum of increase in CapEx may not continue at the same rate. And our view is there based on the leverage that's already been taken out by the big hyperscalers. They just don't have the capital to keep increasing their investing. So we think that the investment level will continue but the growth rate may moderate.
